## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Surāpānajātaka* (Ja 81) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection, bearing the English title *Drinking Liquor*. In the frame narrative (*vatthu*), the Buddha relates the story while residing at the Ghosita park near Kosambī concerning the Elder Sāgata (Sāgatatthera) [Fausböll 1877]. Following a rainy season retreat in Sāvatthī, the Buddha arrived at the market town of Bhaddavatikā [Fausböll 1877]; the background narrative recounts how Elder Sāgata employed his supernatural powers to subdue and convert a deadly poisonous nāga king who attempted to harm him with smoke and fire [Boulton 1982]. Following this victory, lay followers in Kosambī offered intoxicating liquor—specifically described as *kāpotikā surā* or *kāpotikā pasannā* ("white spirits")—which intoxicated the elder [Horner, Vinaya Pitaka vol 2].

The canonical verses open with the words *Apāyimha anaccimha* ("We drank, we danced") [Fausböll 1877]. In the story of the past and its formal conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the assembly of ascetics (*isigaṇa*) in that past life were the present Buddha's disciples (*Buddhaparisā*), while their leader (*gaṇasatthā*) was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1877].
